features.does: The co-op knows whether and how prescription medicines, vapes and other restricted goods could ever be delivered.

parts.name: Restricted goods study
parts.what: The rules for medicines, vapes, tobacco and other restricted goods.

areas.name: Member voting and the open cost ledger
areas.summary: Restaurants and couriers keep all the profit except running costs: they vote on fees and rules, see exactly what it costs to run, and decide where it opens next.

features.name: Vote on fees and rules
features.does: A member proposes and votes on the delivery fee formula, the platform rules and the dispatch rules.

parts.name: Food proposal types
parts.what: What Spare Food members can vote on and who may vote on each, with every courier pay vote passing the competition law check first.

parts.name: Proposal and vote screens
parts.what: Food's proposal summaries, showing what each would change in the fees, on the kit's voting screen.

parts.name: Results become settings
parts.what: Maps each passed Food vote to the setting it changes, applied by the kit.

features.name: A voice for each side
features.does: Couriers decide courier pay, restaurants decide restaurant rules, and both decide shared rules.

parts.name: Who votes on what
parts.what: Food's electorates (couriers, restaurants or both) on the kit's electorates and constitution rules.

parts.name: Business members
parts.what: Who counts as the member when a restaurant is a business: one vote per company, per outlet or per owner, how franchise groups count, and whether staff vote.

parts.name: Competition law gate for pay votes
parts.what: Couriers vote on the delivery fee formula, the busy-time bonus and the waiting rate only in a form the kit's competition law check clears, such as pay set by the co-op as employer, a competition authority's authorisation (example: New Zealand's Commerce Commission), or a collective bargaining law if one applies.

features.name: Open cost ledger
features.does: Anyone can see each month's running cost, the number of orders, and what the fee paid for.

parts.name: Spare Food ledger page
parts.what: Food's monthly costs, order counts and resulting fee on the kit's ledger pages, as open data.

features.name: Surplus lowers the next fee
features.does: Any surplus is shown on the ledger and lowers the next period's fee.

parts.name: Surplus rollover
parts.what: Food's surplus carried into the next fee by the kit's fee setting.

features.name: Learn from other courier co-ops
features.does: A member can read how other courier co-ops ran, what worked and what failed.

parts.name: Courier co-op study
parts.what: How existing courier co-ops run and their software, learning only from code whose licence allows it.

features.name: Open a city
features.does: Members decide where Spare Food opens next, and it opens once enough restaurants, couriers and customers have pledged and signed up.

parts.name: Launch readiness tracker
parts.what: Food's targets for restaurants, couriers and customers in each area, counted on the kit's launch areas before the area opens. The counting should move into the kit's marketplace engine for every marketplace.

parts.name: First city and launch plan
parts.what: Rank cities and plan how to sign up enough restaurants and couriers at the same time.

parts.name: Whether food goes first
parts.what: How Spare Food ranks against the other marketplaces as the first to build.

parts.name: Restaurant outreach and pledges
parts.what: A list of restaurants to approach, and pledges to join once enough others in the area have pledged, on the same shared launch counting.

parts.name: Courier sign-up before launch
parts.what: Couriers apply and pass their checks before an area opens, counted towards its target.

parts.name: Waitlist for unserved addresses
parts.what: Customers at addresses not yet served join a waitlist that counts towards opening their area on the kit's launch areas.

features.name: Member meetings and reports
features.does: A member can read the annual report and take part in member meetings online.

parts.name: Online member meetings
parts.what: Food's papers and votes in the kit's member meetings.

features.name: A reserve for bad months
features.does: Anyone can see a voted reserve for chargebacks, fraud, legal claims and slow months, and how the first months are funded.

parts.name: Food's reserve
parts.what: Food's share and risks (chargebacks, fraud, food sickness claims and slow months) on the kit's voted reserve line, shown on the ledger.

parts.name: Start-up funding
parts.what: How the first months are paid for (donations, loans or grants), shown on the ledger.

features.name: Emergency powers
features.does: Operators can act at once in an emergency, within published limits, and members review every such change afterwards.

parts.name: Emergency powers rules
parts.what: Food's list of emergency changes (pausing zones in a storm, adding a courier bonus, suspending a restaurant after an outbreak) and how long each may last. The emergency powers rule itself belongs with the constitution's voting rules in the kit.

parts.name: Emergency changes with review
parts.what: Each emergency change ends on its own after a set time and goes to members for review.

areas.name: Apps, devices and offline
areas.summary: The three apps on phones, tablets and the web, working on old devices, weak signal and little data.

features.name: Customer app on any phone
features.does: A customer orders from a web app with no install, or from an installed phone app.

parts.name: Food's phone needs
parts.what: Food's needs for the kit's phone app decision: background location for couriers, loud alerts for restaurants and lock-screen status for customers.

parts.name: Customer web app
parts.what: Packs the customer screens from the other areas into the kit's app frame for any browser, with nothing to install.

parts.name: Installed customer app
parts.what: Food's customer app on the kit's installable app wrapper, with push and location.

features.name: Restaurant app on a tablet
features.does: A restaurant runs the app on a cheap tablet, a phone or a computer it already owns.

parts.name: Restaurant app shell
parts.what: Food's restaurant app on the kit's installable app wrapper, keeping the screen awake and playing alerts.

parts.name: Shared kitchen tablets
parts.what: A kitchen tablet signs in to a location, not a person; staff switch by PIN, an owner signs it out remotely from the kit's device list, and payouts, bank details and staff admin never show on it. This shared device mode should move down into the kit, since Spare Market shops need it.

features.name: Courier location in the background
features.does: A courier's app keeps sharing location during a job with the phone locked, within app store rules.

parts.name: Background location
parts.what: Food asks for background location only while a courier is on a job, using the kit's location permissions.

parts.name: Battery and data saver
parts.what: Fewer location updates while the courier is waiting.

features.name: Work through weak signal
features.does: Each app keeps working when the network drops and catches up later.

parts.name: Restaurant offline queue
parts.what: Accept and mark orders while offline, synced in order once back.

parts.name: Customer offline handling
parts.what: Show the last known status and queue messages while offline.

parts.name: Order clash rules
parts.what: Food's outcome for each clash between order changes made offline, such as a cancel while the kitchen marks the order ready, two couriers both delivering after a reassignment, or a refund while the courier confirms delivery.

features.name: Notifications a person chooses
features.does: Each person chooses what reaches them by push, text or email.

parts.name: Notification settings
parts.what: Food's message kinds on the kit's notification settings, with safety notices always on.

features.name: Old phones and slow networks
features.does: The apps load fast on old phones and slow, costly mobile data.

parts.name: Speed and size budget
parts.what: Food's size and speed limits checked on every change, on the kit's light mode for slow connections.

features.name: Courier app on a phone
features.does: A courier installs an app built for a phone cradle that keeps working through a whole shift.

parts.name: Courier app shell
parts.what: Food's courier app on the kit's installable app wrapper, built for a phone cradle, with location on during jobs and the current job's map kept on the phone.

features.name: Maps with no signal
features.does: A courier downloads map areas for places with weak signal.

parts.name: Offline map areas
parts.what: Map areas for Food's zones from the kit's offline map packs, offered to couriers who work there.

areas.name: Accessibility, languages and countries
areas.summary: Usable by everyone, in English and other languages, and ready for any country with its own rules pack; New Zealand is the first, with te reo Māori.

features.name: Accessible apps
features.does: A blind, low-vision, Deaf or motor-impaired person can use every app fully.

parts.name: WCAG 2.2 AA on every screen
parts.what: Food's screens built from the kit's accessible components, and tested with screen readers to WCAG 2.2 AA.

parts.name: Accessibility checks
parts.what: Food's screens in the kit's accessibility testing, plus regular testing with disabled customers, couriers and restaurant staff.

parts.name: Message-only courier option
parts.what: A Deaf or hard-of-hearing courier can ask customers to message instead of calling.

parts.name: Display settings
parts.what: Food's screens follow the kit's text size, contrast and motion settings.

parts.name: Card fields tested too
parts.what: The payment provider's card fields and wallet buttons are tested to the same accessibility standard before a provider is chosen, since checkout runs inside them.

parts.name: Offers seen and felt
parts.what: Offers and alerts are shown large and signalled by vibration as well as read aloud, so Deaf and hard-of-hearing couriers miss nothing.

features.name: Many languages
features.does: A person uses the apps in their own language, starting with English and the languages of each launch country (example: te reo Māori in New Zealand).

parts.name: Food translation files
parts.what: All Food interface text in the kit's translation framework.

parts.name: Launch country languages (example: te reo Māori)
parts.what: A full version in each launch country's own languages, checked by fluent speakers, starting with te reo Māori for New Zealand.

parts.name: Chat translation
parts.what: Food turns on the kit's message translation for chats between couriers, customers and restaurants.

features.name: Other countries
features.does: Spare Food runs in any country with that country's currency, tax, addresses and laws, set in its own country pack.

parts.name: Food country settings
parts.what: Food's settings for each country (delivery rules, alcohol and food law, and units) on the kit's country packs.

parts.name: Food tax per country
parts.what: Food's order lines mapped to the kit's tax rules for each country.

parts.name: Platform work law by country
parts.what: Courier rules in each country, such as the EU Platform Work Directive and Australia's minimum standards for gig workers.

parts.name: Allergen lists per country
parts.what: Allergen lists for each country, such as the EU's 14, the US's 9 and the ANZ list, plus energy units, so allergen data entered in one country fits the others.

features.name: Local formats
features.does: A person sees times, dates, money and addresses in their local way.

parts.name: Locale formatting
parts.what: Food's dates, times, money and addresses through the kit's local formats.

features.name: Courier and kitchen languages
features.does: Couriers and restaurant staff use the apps, and read their terms and safety lessons, in a language they read well.

parts.name: Languages for couriers and kitchens
parts.what: Courier and restaurant apps in the languages their users read most, such as Hindi, Punjabi, Mandarin and Korean, chosen from sign-up figures, through the kit's member translation and machine translation at cost.

parts.name: Terms and lessons in the courier's language
parts.what: Courier terms and safety lessons in the language the courier chose, translated and checked by a person, so no courier agrees to terms they cannot read.

features.name: Right-to-left languages
features.does: A person reads the apps in Arabic, Urdu or another right-to-left language.

parts.name: Right-to-left screens
parts.what: Food's screens on the kit's right-to-left layout.

features.name: Readable receipts and statements
features.does: A screen reader user reads every receipt, statement and invoice from Food.

parts.name: Accessible Food documents
parts.what: Food's receipts, payout statements and tax invoices as the kit's accessible PDFs.

features.name: Easy read and sign language
features.does: A person reads the key steps in easy-read text, or watches them in the country's sign language (example: New Zealand Sign Language).

parts.name: Food easy read and sign language
parts.what: Easy-read text and videos in each country's sign language (example: NZ Sign Language) for ordering, signing up to deliver and reporting a problem, on the kit's easy read and sign language.

areas.name: Privacy, data and legal duties
areas.summary: Members control their data and can take it with them, and the app meets every law that applies to a food platform.

features.name: Take or delete my data
features.does: A person downloads all their data in open formats, or has it deleted.

parts.name: Food data export
parts.what: Food's orders, messages, ratings, payouts and settings added to the kit's data export.

parts.name: Open data formats
parts.what: Published formats for orders, menus and payouts.

parts.name: Food retention rules
parts.what: Food's keeping times for orders, chats, photos and payouts, on the kit's retention schedules and account deletion.

features.name: Know who answers for food safety
features.does: A customer, restaurant or courier can see which food safety duties sit with the restaurant, the courier and the platform.

parts.name: Food rules study
parts.what: What the restaurant is responsible for and what the platform is, with sources.

parts.name: Food safety duties page
parts.what: A plain page, linked from the terms and the help centre, showing who answers for what under food safety law (example: New Zealand's Food Act).

features.name: Courier status and pay law
features.does: Courier terms meet employment law, including each country's test for who is a contractor (example: New Zealand's 2026 gateway test), or couriers are employed.

parts.name: Courier status for Food
parts.what: Food's facts for the kit's worker status test, such as who sets pay, who controls hours and whether couriers work for others, and the result set in the kit's worker status per app, decided with a lawyer.

parts.name: Accident cover and insurance
parts.what: Public accident cover and its levies (example: New Zealand's ACC), and insurance options for couriers.

features.name: Privacy law duties
features.does: The app meets privacy law (example: New Zealand's Privacy Act 2020): clear notices, access and correction requests, and breach reporting.

parts.name: Food privacy policy
parts.what: Food's own sections of the privacy policy and request flow, on the kit's privacy page, terms and breach response.

parts.name: Location data limits
parts.what: Food's location rules on the kit's live location: shared only during a job and not kept afterwards, unless the law, safety or a dispute needs a trace.

parts.name: Indirect collection notices
parts.what: Notices for every indirect collection in Food (example: New Zealand's privacy principle 3A): licence, criminal record and identity results from providers, customer details supplied by restaurants, and proof photos that show other people.

parts.name: Food privacy impact assessments
parts.what: Privacy impact assessments, on the kit's template and register, for live location, selfie checks, allergy and access data, and proof photos, before each is built.

parts.name: Food's outside processors
parts.what: Food's outside processors, such as masked calls, identity checks, texts and the payment provider, on the kit's processor list, with the overseas checks for each.

parts.name: Police requests for Food data
parts.what: Requests from police and courts for courier traces, addresses and order records, handled through the kit's law enforcement request process and counted in public.

features.name: Consent for marketing
features.does: A person only gets marketing messages they agreed to, as the anti-spam law requires.

parts.name: Consent records
parts.what: Food's marketing consents on the kit's consent records.

features.name: Terms and policies
features.does: Customers, restaurants and couriers agree to clear terms that avoid unfair contract terms.

parts.name: Customer terms
parts.what: Plain-English terms of use.

parts.name: Restaurant terms
parts.what: Terms for restaurants checked against the unfair contract terms rules.

parts.name: Courier terms
parts.what: Food's courier terms on the kit's contractor agreements, or an employment agreement if couriers are employees, matching the status decision.

parts.name: Terms versions
parts.what: Food's terms versions on the kit's terms and policy versions.

features.name: Records the law requires
features.does: The co-op keeps tax, payment and anti-money-laundering records for as long as the law requires.

parts.name: Food records
parts.what: Food's records and how long each is kept, on the kit's financial record keeping.

features.name: Limits on who sees customer data
features.does: A customer's details are seen only by those who need them, and only while they need them.

parts.name: Restaurant data rules
parts.what: What a restaurant sees and may keep (a name, a masked phone, and an address only for its own-courier orders), with each restaurant treated as its own privacy agency.

parts.name: Details hidden after the job
parts.what: Hides the customer's name and address from the courier once the job ends, and limits restaurant views by staff role.

features.name: Leave with my business
features.does: A restaurant or courier leaving the platform takes its menu, records and reputation with it.

parts.name: Restaurant export
parts.what: The menu in an open format, plus orders, reviews and the followers who agreed to it.

parts.name: Courier reputation export
parts.what: A signed copy of a courier's ratings, from the kit's portable reputation.

parts.name: Leaving rules
parts.what: A notice period, a final payout, and what happens to direct-ordering links and QR codes.

features.name: Care with health, faith and disability details
features.does: A person's allergies, faith-based diets and access needs are saved only with consent, shared only as much as each order needs, and deleted in one step.

parts.name: Sensitive details rules
parts.what: Rules for health, religious and disability details: consent before saving, the least detail each party needs, no use in suggestions unless switched on, one-step deletion, and treatment as special category data where the GDPR applies. The kit should hold one such rule for every app.

parts.name: Least detail per order
parts.what: Maps each saved need to the instruction each party sees on an order, such as 'bring it to the door' for the courier and the allergens for the kitchen, and nothing more.

areas.name: Operations and admin
areas.summary: The tools the co-op's small team and member volunteers use to run each city safely and at cost, built on the kit's admin console, monitoring and status page.

features.name: Operations console
features.does: An operator sees live orders, couriers online and problems across a city.

parts.name: Live operations view
parts.what: Food's live map and list of active orders, courier supply and late orders, in the kit's admin console.

parts.name: Operator actions
parts.what: Pause a zone, reassign a job or contact a party, each logged as an operation.

features.name: Review queues
features.does: Staff and volunteers work through applications, reports, menu checks and claims in one place.

parts.name: Food review queue types
parts.what: Food's queues (applications, menu checks and claims) in the kit's moderation queue and admin console.

features.name: Admin roles and audit
features.does: Every admin action is limited to its role and logged for members to inspect.

parts.name: Admin roles
parts.what: Food's staff and volunteer roles, least access by default, on the kit's permission checks and access controls.

parts.name: Admin audit log
parts.what: Every Food admin action in the operation log through the kit's admin console, open to member auditors.

features.name: Monitoring and incidents
features.does: The team knows when something breaks and fixes it fast, and uptime is published.

parts.name: Food monitoring
parts.what: Food's checks for payment failures and dispatch delays on the kit's monitoring and alerts.

parts.name: Incident playbooks
parts.what: Food's playbooks for payments, maps or dispatch failing in the middle of dinner, in the kit's incident response.

parts.name: Status page
parts.what: Food on the kit's status page, with public uptime and incidents.

parts.name: City-by-city releases
parts.what: New versions reach one city at a time, using the kit's feature switches.

parts.name: No updates mid-service
parts.what: Restaurant tablets and courier apps never reload for an update while orders are open or a job is under way; updates wait for a quiet moment, on the kit's update delivery.

features.name: City simulator
features.does: The team runs a whole city of simulated orders to test dispatch before launch.

parts.name: City simulation
parts.what: Food's simulated restaurants, kitchens and couriers, run on a shared city simulator to test dispatch rules and load. The simulator itself should move down into the kit, since Spare Ride maps the same.

features.name: Self-hosting
features.does: A member group runs its own Spare Food servers for its area.

parts.name: Self-host package
parts.what: Food's settings and guides on the kit's self-host package.

features.name: Security checked before each city
features.does: Each city opens only after outside testers have checked Food's own attack list.

parts.name: Food threat model
parts.what: Food's attack list: guessing hand-over codes, promo and referral abuse, fake restaurants, rented courier accounts, faked GPS, SIM swaps and recycled numbers, a stolen or shared kitchen tablet, courier and customer collusion, scripted refund claims, scraping of menus and addresses, and stalking through location data.

parts.name: Outside test before each launch
parts.what: An outside security test against the threat model before each city opens.

features.name: Severe weather and emergencies
features.does: Operators see weather and emergency management warnings (example: New Zealand's Civil Defence), and can switch a city into an emergency mode.

parts.name: Weather and emergency warnings
parts.what: Weather warnings and emergency management alerts shown to operators, with suggested zone pauses, from a shared feed the kit should own, since Spare Ride, Spare Stay and Spare Work need it too. Each country has its own sources; for New Zealand, Civil Defence and MetService, whose data terms are *unverified*.

parts.name: Emergency mode
parts.what: Pauses or shrinks zones, tells couriers and customers why, and ends on its own when the warning lifts.

areas.name: Headless: AI, plugins and open interface
areas.summary: Everything a person can do, an AI agent or a script can do through the same commands, and restaurants can add sandboxed plugins.

features.name: Command interface
features.does: Every action in every Spare Food app is a command a script can call.

parts.name: Food command frame
parts.what: The shared shape of Food's commands and queries on the kit's command schemas: naming, versions, errors and permissions, split by area into the command sets below.

parts.name: Interface reference and keys
parts.what: Food's published command reference, with access keys per restaurant on the kit's API keys.

parts.name: Command coverage check
parts.what: A check on every change that each action on a Food screen has a matching command.

parts.name: Menu and restaurant commands
parts.what: Commands and queries for menus, stock, hours, pauses and restaurant staff.

parts.name: Order commands
parts.what: Commands and queries for carts, checkout, order steps, changes and cancels.

parts.name: Courier job commands
parts.what: Commands and queries for going online, offers, pickup, drop-off and earnings.

parts.name: Money commands
parts.what: Commands and queries for payouts, refunds, tips and statements.

parts.name: Support, dispute and review commands
parts.what: Commands and queries for problem reports, support cases, disputes, ratings and reviews.

parts.name: Member commands
parts.what: Commands and queries for Food proposals, votes and the ledger.

parts.name: Operator and admin commands
parts.what: Commands and queries for zones, review queues, operator actions and admin roles.

features.name: Order through an AI assistant
features.does: A customer asks an AI assistant to order dinner, and confirms before any money moves.

parts.name: Spare Food MCP server
parts.what: Food's search, order and track tools on the kit's MCP server.

parts.name: Payment confirmation guard
parts.what: Any order an AI places waits for the person's approval before payment, using Food's approval list on the kit's approval steps.

parts.name: Allergies and swaps stay with the person
parts.what: An order an agent places always carries the person's saved allergy request, and a kitchen's allergy decline, a swap offer or an allergy question goes back to the person, never answered by the agent.

features.name: AI help for restaurants
features.does: A restaurant asks an assistant to update the menu, read sales or pause for an hour.

parts.name: Restaurant MCP tools
parts.what: Menu, hours and report tools for staff's AI assistants, limited to each person's role.

features.name: Plugins
features.does: A restaurant or member adds sandboxed plugins, such as a point-of-sale link or a loyalty card.

parts.name: Food plugin hooks
parts.what: Hooks for order events, menu sync and pricing, with declared permissions.

features.name: Order event notices
features.does: A restaurant's own systems are told about new and changed orders as they happen.

parts.name: Order webhooks
parts.what: Food's order events sent through the kit's signed webhooks.

features.name: Fair rules for scripts and agents
features.does: Scripts and AI agents can help couriers and customers, but never grab jobs ahead of people or spend money without a person's approval.

parts.name: Courier command limits
parts.what: Food's rules on the kit's automated acceptance rules: courier scripts may go online and export earnings, but never accept offers automatically, so bots never beat people to jobs.

parts.name: Commands that need approval
parts.what: The Food commands that always need a person's approval: placing an order, tipping, a late cancel, accepting a swap, changing the address after pickup, a refund claim, a gift order, price changes and payout changes.

parts.name: People-only Food actions
parts.what: Ratings, reviews, votes, dispute statements and alcohol age declarations come only from the person, never an agent, on the kit's people-only actions.

parts.name: Agent labels for restaurants and couriers
parts.what: Orders, messages and changes an agent makes carry the kit's agent label, so the restaurant and the courier see they came from an agent acting for a named person.

parts.name: Agent limits, sign-in and activity
parts.what: Food's spending limits for each agent on the kit's agent limits, agent sign-in under the MCP authorisation rules, and a list of every agent action in Food, with undo where it can be undone.

parts.name: Scraping limits
parts.what: No bulk copying of menus, addresses, reviews or courier details through Food's command API or MCP tools, on the kit's bulk copy limits.

assess: Could a customer, a restaurant and a courier each finish a whole order, from sign-up to payout, using only the core features?
Does every feature a regular Uber Eats, DoorDash or local delivery app user relies on each week have a home in this map, and does each reason in the left-out list (the last question) still hold?

Is the courier status decision (FD02) settled before courier terms, pay, ratings and removal are built, since it changes all of them, and does every courier pay vote pass the competition law check (KIT-A12-F4-P3) first?
Does the price breakdown make it obvious what the restaurant, the courier, the running cost and sales tax each get, so a customer trusts it more than the big apps?
Is the at-cost fee believable in the first months, when the running cost is shared over few orders?
Does ready-timed dispatch (FD03) have a proven, published method to port, or is it being invented?
Will restaurants accept a separate tablet at launch, or must point-of-sale and printer links (FD05) come first?
Which parts are shared with Spare Ride (courier accounts, location, routing, safety) and are they moved down into the kit rather than copied?

Is each legal duty in the first country pack (for New Zealand: Food Act, GST on listed services, income reporting, anti-money-laundering, Privacy Act, alcohol) covered by a piece and checked by a lawyer before launch?
Are groceries, alcohol and catering rightly marked later, given the extra law and the picker app they need?
Can every screen in the demo be used with a keyboard and a screen reader, and in each launch country's languages (example: te reo Māori)?
Does anything in the demo look like an incumbent's interface, name, colours or icons?
What does the demo show when the courier's or the restaurant's signal drops mid-order?
How does the co-op sign up enough restaurants and couriers in one city at the same time, and what count is enough to open?
Which large parts should be split further before the Design stage, and is any size clearly wrong?
Are the decisions on what the at-cost fee may cover (FOOD-A9-F2-P3) and who pays it (FOOD-A9-F2-P4) made before the price calculator, the money split and the ledger page are built?

Does the demo show what happens when an order goes wrong: a declined or unanswered order, a silent restaurant tablet, an allergy request the kitchen declines, and a report of sickness or an allergic reaction?

Food's core features rest on kit parts the kit marks as next or later: organisation model (KIT-A1-F7-P1, next); team management (KIT-A1-F7-P2, next); vehicle checks (KIT-A2-F6-P2, next); business number lookup (KIT-A2-F7-P1, next); trader details (KIT-A2-F7-P2, next); background checks (KIT-A2-F9-P1, next); background check link (KIT-A2-F9-P2, next); face check fairness testing (KIT-A2-F12-P1, next); repeat face checks (KIT-A2-F12-P2, next); sanctions screening (KIT-A4-F8-P1, later); scheduled and repeat bookings (KIT-A5-F9-P1, next); multi-party orders (KIT-A5-F11-P1, next); favourites (KIT-A5-F12-P1, next); order changes (KIT-A5-F15-P1, next); fairness checks (KIT-A6-F5-P2, next); turn-by-turn guidance (KIT-A7-F6-P1, next); message translation (KIT-A8-F7-P1, next); fraud signals (KIT-A10-F12-P2, next); insurance claims link (KIT-A11-F9-P2, later); privacy impact assessments (KIT-A18-F10-P1, next); update delivery (KIT-A20-F7-P1, next). Will the kit bring each one forward, or should the Food part that needs it wait?
Which Food parts still have no work-board piece, such as the first city and launch plan, start-up funding, insurance and restricted goods, and should new pieces be opened for them?

Food asks the kit to open shared parts it does not have yet: a shared worker record of hours across apps (FOOD-A6-F1-P4); a shared device mode for kitchen and shop tablets (FOOD-A16-F2-P2); an A-to-B delivery job type (FOOD-A14-F5-P1, FOOD-A14-F6-P1); a guest order decision (FOOD-A1-F1-P6); union access and bargaining duties (FOOD-A6-F13-P7); a sales tax threshold warning (FOOD-A10-F13-P1); rules for health, faith and disability details (FOOD-A18-F10-P1); access needs on the profile (FOOD-A4-F13-P1); a shop page and a till (FOOD-A13-F4-P1, FOOD-A13-F5-P1); a mileage and expense log (FOOD-A6-F6-P4); text and phone ordering (FOOD-A4-F14-P1, FOOD-A4-F14-P2); a driving-safe mode and the phone road rules (FOOD-A6-F12-P1, FOOD-A6-F12-P3); tax withholding from payouts (FOOD-A10-F11-P1, FOOD-A10-F11-P2); a city simulator (FOOD-A19-F5-P1); emergency powers rules (FOOD-A15-F9-P1); a weather and emergency warnings feed (FOOD-A19-F8-P1); launch counting, pledges and waitlists (FOOD-A15-F6-P1, FOOD-A15-F6-P4, FOOD-A15-F6-P6). Has the kit opened each one, so the Food part becomes a thin use of it?

Left out on purpose: paid placement and ads (rankings follow published rules and are never sold); paid subscriptions (member benefits in FOOD-A9-F8 lower fees instead, if members vote for them); a paid priority delivery tier (dispatch treats every order by the same published rules); co-op-run dark stores (the co-op runs no kitchens or shops of its own and serves independent sellers); drones and robots (not proven at scale, and tightly limited by aviation and road rules); table reservations (a booking product, not delivery, which can come later as its own feature or app); package returns (returns belong with a shared delivery job type in the kit and with Spare Market's shipping); restaurant cash advances and loans (lending brings in credit law and is not an at-cost running cost). Does each reason still hold?
